svg.title: A tagged trunk between two switches, the four settings that matter, and the overwrite accident that takes out three hundred phones
svg.desc: Two switches joined by a tagged trunk, with the VLAN tag fields shown and four VLANs riding the link: native, data, voice and management. Four design points beside it: write down the native VLAN on both ends, build the allowed list with add rather than a bare list, prune transit VLANs but never management, and remember that the VLAN count is the blast radius. A note at the bottom describes the common accident, a bare allowed vlan command that removes voice and management from the trunk and takes out three hundred phones, and the change-control habit of capturing the configuration before and diffing after.
svg.text: A trunk is one cable carrying many failure domains, and two settings decide which ones leak
The tag is not a label, it is a promise about who can reach whom
SW-1
SW-2
802.1Q trunk
DA · SA
TPID 8100
PCP
DEI
VID 12 bits
the tag, and the path it implies
one frame, four fields that decide its VLAN and its priority
1 native
10 data
20 voice
99 mgmt
... whatever the list allows
An untagged frame arrives on the native VLAN. If the two ends disagree,
that frame lands in a VLAN it was never meant to reach, silently.
FOUR SETTINGS THAT DECIDE EVERYTHING
1. Native VLAN, written on both ends
A mismatch bridges two VLANs with no error. Set it explicitly, and never
leave it at the default while the other end has been changed.
2. The allowed list, always with add
A bare list replaces the whole set: everything you did not repeat is
removed from the trunk, including VLANs nobody remembered.
3. Prune transit VLANs, never management
Pruning is bandwidth hygiene. Pruning management is how you lose the
ability to reach the device you just changed.
4. The VLAN count is the blast radius
Whatever rides this trunk can be affected by a loop on the other end.
Fewer VLANs per trunk is a reliability decision, not a housekeeping one.
THE ACCIDENT THIS SECTION EXISTS FOR
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
intended as "add 20", executed as "only 10 and 20" — voice and management removed, three hundred phones drop, and the change ticket is closed as successful.
The prevention is a habit, not a command: capture the running configuration before the change, diff it after, and put the diff in the ticket.
A trunk is a contract between two switches that never read the same document. Both ends must be configured, both ends must be verified, and neither end knows what the other was told.
That is why trunks belong in templates and in monitoring: a mismatch is invisible in the configuration of either side taken alone.
The check that catches it is a diff between the two ends, run by a script, not by a person at two in the morning.
